prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My mother loves butter more than I do, more than anyone. She pulls chunks off the stick and eats it plain, explaining cream spun around into butter! Growing up we ate turkey cutlets sauteed in lemon and butter, butter and cheese on green noodles, butter melting in small pools in the hearts of Yorkshire puddings, butter better than gravy staining white rice yellow, butter glazing corn in slipping squares, butter the lava in white volcanoes of hominy grits, butter softening in a white bowl to be creamed with white sugar, butter disappearing into whipped sweet potatoes, with pineapple, butter melted and curdy to pour over pancakes, butter licked off the plate with warm Alaga syrup. When I picture the good old days I am grinning greasy with my brother, having watched the tiger chase his tail and turn to butter. We are Mumbo and Jumbo’s children despite historical revision, despite our parent’s efforts, glowing from the inside out, one hundred megawatts of butter.

Butter holds a special place in my mother's heart—even greater than mine, greater than anyone's. She breaks off pieces from the stick to eat unadorned, always noting how cream gets churned into butter! In my childhood home, turkey cutlets sizzled in lemon and butter, cheese and butter coated green noodles, and butter pooled in tiny lakes within the craters of Yorkshire puddings. Butter, superior to gravy, tinted white rice golden; it glazed corn in melting squares and served as molten lava cascading down white peaks of hominy grits. I remember butter left to soften in a white bowl before being whipped together with white sugar, butter vanishing into whipped sweet potatoes mixed with pineapple, butter melted into curds and poured over pancakes, and butter licked straight from the plate alongside warm Alaga syrup.

When nostalgia strikes, I picture myself grinning with greasy satisfaction beside my brother, both of us having witnessed that tiger circle round and transform into butter. Regardless of how history gets rewritten, regardless of our parents' attempts otherwise, we remain the offspring of Mumbo and Jumbo—radiant from within, shining with a hundred megawatts of pure butter.
outputs.L3:
My mother loves butter the way other people love chocolate or coffee—unapologetically, almost devotionally. I have watched her unwrap a stick of butter, cut off a small pat, and eat it plain, standing at the kitchen counter as though it were the most natural snack in the world. To her, butter needs no vehicle, no bread or cracker to justify its presence. It is complete on its own, a food worthy of being savored for its own sake.

Growing up, that reverence for butter shaped nearly every meal that came out of our kitchen. It wasn't confined to one category of cooking; it moved fluidly between savory and sweet, weaving itself into the fabric of our everyday diet. Turkey cutlets were seared in butter until their edges turned golden and crisp. Rice was never simply steamed—it was finished with a generous knob of butter stirred in until it melted into a glossy, fragrant sheen. And then there were the sweeter dishes: pancakes stacked high and pooled with melted butter before the syrup ever touched them, and whipped sweet potatoes, fluffed and folded with so much butter that they turned almost custard-like, rich enough to be dessert in their own right. Butter wasn't an afterthought or a garnish in our house. It was a foundation, a philosophy of cooking passed down without ever being explicitly taught.

Some of my fondest memories are of sitting at the table with my brother, forks in hand, racing to see who could get to the buttery mashed potatoes first, or arguing over who deserved the last pancake soaked in butter and syrup. Those meals feel, in retrospect, like small rituals of childhood—simple, warm, and unremarkable in the moment, but glowing now with the soft light of nostalgia. When I think back on "the good old days," it is often through the lens of food: the smell of butter melting in a hot pan, the clatter of plates, my brother laughing at something silly across the table. Butter, in this way, became more than an ingredient. It became a marker of home.

But there is another layer to this love of butter, one that is harder to talk about and impossible to ignore. The phrase "the tiger turned to butter" comes from *Little Black Sambo*, a story with a complicated and painful legacy. Written in 1899, the book has long been criticized for its racist caricatures, even as its central image—tigers chasing each other around a tree until they melt into a pool of butter—remained oddly enchanting to generations of children, including, apparently, my own parents. The story's shadow lingers uncomfortably close to home: my parents, whether as an inside joke or an act of reclamation, sometimes referred to my brother and me as "Mumbo and Jumbo's children," names lifted directly from the tale's problematic origins.

I think about this legacy often, especially as more of the story's history has been revisited and revised over the years, with many editions rewritten or removed from shelves in an effort to distance children from its racist undertones. My parents, in their own way, tried to shield us from the uglier parts of that history, letting the "butter" imagery remain playful and light rather than burdened by its origins. And yet, I cannot fully separate the two. To embrace the nickname "Mumbo and Jumbo's children" is to hold both truths at once: the innocence of a shared family joke, and the weight of a story rooted in caricature and harm.

Still, I find that I do not want to discard the joy simply because the history is complicated. Instead, I choose to hold both—the love of butter that shaped my childhood table, and the acknowledgment of where some of that language came from. There is something powerful in taking a story meant to diminish and finding, within it, a source of identity and even humor. To call ourselves "Mumbo and Jumbo's children" is not to erase the discomfort of the reference, but to insist that our joy, our nostalgia, and our sense of self cannot be reduced to someone else's caricature. Butter, in our family, became a symbol of comfort reclaimed—melting, golden, and entirely our own.

# The Butter of My People

My mother loved butter the way some women love pearls or perfume—extravagantly, unapologetically, as if it were her birthright. She kept it soft on the counter in a dish shaped like a hen, the yellow mound glistening under a glass dome, always ready, always waiting to be summoned into service. There was no meal in our house that butter did not touch, no dish it could not improve, no morning it did not begin.

I remember the turkey cutlets my mother fried on Sunday afternoons, dredged in flour and pan-seared in a skillet slicked with butter until the edges turned the color of caramel, until the kitchen filled with a smell that meant *home* before the word had even formed in my mouth. She would drop another pat on top just before serving, watching it melt into the meat's warm surface like a blessing being administered.

The grits were the same—white and steaming in the pot, and then the butter went in, not a teaspoon but a generous knifeful, stirred until the whole pot turned glossy and rich, until you could see your own reflection faintly in the sheen of it. My mother said grits without butter were "just wet sand," and she said it with the conviction of a woman stating a fact of nature, like gravity or the changing of seasons.

Pancakes came stacked high on Saturday mornings, and butter did not simply sit on top—it was folded between each layer, so that by the time the syrup arrived, everything was already swimming, already rich, already perfect. My siblings and I would watch the butter slide down the sides of the stack in slow, golden rivulets, and there was a kind of reverence in that watching, a communion we didn't yet have words for.

Toast, biscuits, cornbread, rice—everything passed through my mother's hands and came out buttered, transformed, elevated from mere food into something closer to love made edible. She did not measure. She did not apologize. She simply believed, with her whole heart, that butter was the difference between eating and *feasting*, between a meal and a memory.

It was only later, reading the old stories, that I encountered the tale of Little Black Sambo and the tigers who chased each other around a tree until they melted into butter—a story meant, in its original ugly context, to shame and diminish, to reduce Black children to caricature and consumption. But I could not help thinking of my mother's hen-shaped butter dish, of the way she moved through her kitchen like a woman conducting an orchestra of golden, dripping abundance, and I felt something shift in me.

What if those tigers weren't running in fear or humiliation, but in pure, ecstatic motion—dancing themselves into something rich and radiant and essential? What if the butter at the center of that old, wounding story was not a mark of shame but a symbol of transformation, of power distilled into its most nourishing form? My mother's love, after all, had always worked that way—taking whatever she had, however humble, and turning it luminous, golden, unmistakably *hers*.

I come from a family who understood, long before I had language for it, that butter was not excess but essence—that richness was our inheritance, our comfort, our joy. And so I choose now to remember those tigers not as symbols of ridicule but as ancestors of a kind, spinning themselves into gold, into butter, into something my mother would recognize instantly and serve without hesitation, generously, at every single meal.

# Growing Up in Yorkshire

She remembers the moors best—wide stretches of purple heather rolling toward a horizon that seemed to promise something just beyond reach. Growing up in Yorkshire meant learning to read the sky before anyone taught her to read a book, watching clouds gather over the hills and knowing, with the certainty only a child raised outdoors can have, when to run for shelter and when to stay out and let the rain soak through her jumper.

She was shaped by stone walls that had stood for centuries, by villages where everyone knew her name and her grandmother's name before that. Growing up meant Sunday walks along the dales, wellington boots caked in mud, and the particular silence of a countryside that wasn't empty but full—full of sheep calls, wind through grass, the distant rumble of a tractor.

Yorkshire gave her a certain bluntness, too, a way of speaking that didn't waste words but meant every one of them. She learned resilience from a place that battled harsh winters and unpredictable summers, where warmth came from coal fires and strong tea rather than guaranteed sunshine. The people there had a dry humor, an understated kindness that revealed itself slowly, like frost melting off a windowpane.

Now, when she thinks of home, she doesn't picture a single house or street. She pictures the whole landscape—the drystone walls, the grazing sheep, the church spires rising from small towns tucked into valleys. Growing up in Yorkshire wasn't just where she lived; it became part of how she saw everything after, a quiet standard against which all other places were measured and, more often than not, found wanting.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about butter and family food memories, weaving in childhood nostalgia and cultural references.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Butter Dish

There was always a dish of it on the counter, softening under a glass dome like something sacred kept at room temperature, kept ready. My grandmother believed refrigeration was for cowards and Protestants, though we were neither, just people who understood that butter should yield to a knife the way a good memory yields to being told again.

I am talking about the yellow of it. The particular gold that Land O'Lakes promised on cardboard boxes, that maiden kneeling in the reeds while my mother sang along to the radio and cracked eggs one-handed, a trick I never learned, a trick that died with certain kitchens. I am talking about the sound of the toaster's small violence, and then the knife, and then that first bite that was really just butter on bread, poor man's food, rich man's comfort, my grandfather eating it plain some mornings like communion, like he was still nine years old in a house with less.

Bring back the smell of it melting into rice—my mother's mother's trick, a spoonful stirred into the pot after draining, before the lid went back on to let it steam into something silken. This was not a recipe. This was inheritance. This was how you loved someone without saying the word, how you said *I have enough now, so you will have enough too.*

There is a scene in every family's private cinema: someone standing at a stove, wooden spoon in hand, the butter foaming in the pan the way Julia Child taught a nation of housewives to let it foam, to not be afraid of the fat, of the flavor, of taking up space on the plate. My mother watched those reruns like scripture. She said butter doesn't lie to you. She said margarine was for people who didn't trust themselves.

I remember the church potlucks, the butter cookies stamped with a fork's tines, criss-crossed like a secret code only grandmothers knew how to write. I remember the corn on the cob, dripping, the ritual of the roll, the way summer tasted like a stick of butter left out too long in June, going soft in its paper, going generous.

And I remember losing people the way butter disappears into hot bread—slowly, then all at once, then just a stain of warmth left behind, a richness you can still taste if you close your eyes and remember whose hands buttered your toast first, whose hands taught your hands to hold a knife like this, like this, like love is just paying attention to how something softens, how something spreads, how far a small, golden thing can go when you let it sit out, when you let it warm, when you finally let yourself take enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short reflective piece about your mother's love of butter, incorporating vivid descriptions of home-cooked meals from your childhood.
counterfactuals.output:
# Butter

My mother measured love in tablespoons of butter, though she never called it that. She called it "just enough" while her hands added what looked like plenty.

I remember the kitchen on winter mornings, fogged with the smell of butter melting into cast iron, the pan hissing awake as she cracked eggs into it. She'd swirl the pan just so, letting the butter brown slightly at the edges—"That's where the flavor lives," she'd say, though I didn't understand what she meant until years later, standing in my own kitchen, reaching instinctively for more than the recipe called for.

Sunday mornings meant biscuits, and biscuits meant butter folded into flour with her fingertips, cold cubes disappearing into soft dough, then more butter melted and brushed across the tops the moment they emerged golden from the oven. She never leveled the measuring spoon. There was always a little mound, a little extra, because "level" felt like holding back, and holding back wasn't in her nature when it came to feeding the people she loved.

Corn on the cob in August came slathered thick, kernels glistening, butter running down between her fingers as she handed me my ear across the table. Mashed potatoes weren't potatoes at all, really—they were vehicles for butter, whipped until they held little pools of gold in their centers before I even reached for more.

I used to tease her about it. "Do you think butter solves everything?" I'd ask.

She'd just smile and say, "Doesn't it, though?"

Now, older, cooking in a kitchen she'll never stand in, I understand what she meant. Butter was never really about butter. It was about abundance, about never wanting the people at her table to feel like there wasn't enough—of food, of care, of her. Each pat melting into vegetables, each brushstroke across warm bread, was a small, wordless declaration: *I have more to give than the recipe requires, so let me give it.*

I add extra butter now too, more than sensible, more than needed. Not because I've forgotten the calories, but because some inheritances aren't meant to be measured—they're meant to be tasted, again and again, until the recipe becomes memory, and the memory becomes love with a face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a personal essay excerpt exploring food, family, and identity, referencing "Little Black Sambo" imagery in a reclaiming way.
counterfactuals.output:
# Pancakes

My grandmother kept a stack of butter-yellow pancakes coming every Sunday morning, and it wasn't until I was maybe nine that someone at school first connected the food on my plate to a book they'd found in their own grandparents' attic. They said the words like they were handing me something contaminated. *Little Black Sambo.* I didn't understand yet what they meant to do with it, only that suddenly a food I loved felt like it had teeth.

I went home and asked my grandmother about it. She was quiet for a long moment, her hands still moving over the batter, and then she told me what I didn't know: that the story, in its original telling, before it was stolen and redrawn and made grotesque by white illustrators who couldn't imagine Black children as anything but caricature, was about a clever boy in India who outsmarted four tigers and ended up with a stack of pancakes as his reward. The tigers, vain and quarrelsome, chased each other around a tree until they melted into butter. That part, at least, was a story about wit surviving greed.

"They took a boy who won," she said, "and turned him into a joke. That's the part you get to be angry about. Not the syrup."

I think about that distinction often now, the difference between the thing itself and what violence has been done to its image. So much of growing up Black in this country is learning to excavate—to dig past the caricature that someone else painted over your grandmother's kitchen, over your food, your hair, your laughter, and find what was actually there before the theft. The pancakes were never the problem. The tigers running in circles until they became something useful, something sweet—that was never the problem either. The problem was always the hands that took a story of cunning and turned it into a mask, then handed the mask back to us and called it our face.

Now when I make pancakes—and I make them often, my grandmother's recipe, a little too much vanilla, the way she always did it—I think of Sambo outsmarting the tigers. Not the bug-eyed thing on the cover of that old book, but the boy underneath, before the theft, quick enough to turn four beasts' vanity against them and walk away rich in butter and story both. I am descended from people who have always known how to do this: take what was meant to consume us and instead consume it, right down to the fat, and lick the plate clean.

My grandmother is gone now. But her batter recipe lives in my hands exactly as she taught it, and some mornings, flipping pancakes in my own kitchen, I swear I can still hear her voice, telling me which part of the story was mine to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an evocative, sensory-rich passage about growing up in a Southern or Black American household centered on butter as a symbol of love and abundance.
counterfactuals.output:
The butter dish sat on the counter, never in the refrigerator, because Grandma said cold butter was a sin against biscuits. It lived under a glass dome shaped like a hen, and by mid-morning it had gone soft and golden, ready to surrender itself to whatever bread came calling.

She buttered everything like she was arguing with scarcity, like she remembered a time when there wasn't enough and had decided there would never be that time again in her kitchen. Cornbread got a slab thick enough to leave teeth marks. Grits got a whole tablespoon stirred in until they turned glossy as a church shoe. Even the rice, plain white rice, got a knob melted into its center, a little lake of gold pooling in the well she'd press with the back of a spoon.

"Butter makes it worth eating," she'd say, and there was theology in that sentence, something about how plain things deserved to be made rich, how you didn't have to apologize for wanting more than bare survival on your plate.

Saturday mornings, the whole house smelled like her hands—butter and flour and the particular sweetness of vanilla extract, and I'd wake to the sound of her humming something between a hymn and a lullaby while she rolled out biscuit dough soft as a baby's cheek. She cut them with a jelly jar because that's what her mother used, and before they even hit the oven, she'd brush the tops with melted butter using a pastry brush worn down to nothing, bristles splayed like an old woman's hair.

We ate them straight from the pan, too hot, burning our fingers, tearing them open to let more butter melt into the steam. My cousins and I would fight over the corner biscuits, the ones with extra crust, extra butter pooled in their crags.

Nobody in that house went without. Nobody left the table hungry, not for food, not for love—and butter, that soft yellow proof of abundance, was how she said the things her mouth sometimes couldn't.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness style piece listing all the ways butter appeared in your family's cooking, ending with a reflection on heritage and joy.
counterfactuals.output:
# Butter

Butter in the cast iron skillet, melting before the eggs go in, that hiss and foam, my grandmother's wooden spoon pushing it around the edges so nothing sticks, butter for eyes she'd say when it browned just right—butter in the grits, a whole tablespoon disappearing into the steam, stirred until it disappeared into gold—butter on cornbread straight from the oven, cutting a square and watching it melt into all those little pockets, butter on the biscuits too, always cold butter cut into flour with her fingers, quick quick quick before it got warm, the secret to flaky she said, the secret to everything—butter in the pot when the greens went in, just a little bit to round out the vinegar and pepper flakes, butter swirled into gravy at the very end, off heat, that trick to make it glossy—butter for popcorn on Friday nights, melted in a little pot and drizzled not poured, drizzled in three passes so every kernel got some—butter on toast in the morning, butter on pancakes with syrup pooling in the butter-melt divots, butter creamed with sugar for a hundred birthday cakes, the mixer whirring and her humming along to it—butter in pie crust, that flaky secret again, cold cubes of it disappearing into flour like little presents—butter melted and poured over sweet potatoes with brown sugar and cinnamon at Thanksgiving, butter on dinner rolls passed around the table, everyone reaching, butter left out on the counter in its dish with the glass lid, always soft, always ready, never quite enough and always plenty—

and I think about how she never measured it, just knew, the way her hands knew flour and heat and time, the way butter was never indulgence but foundation, the base note under every dish, and how funny that something so simple—cream churned into fat, nothing fancy, no spice rack mystery—could carry so much: her hands, her kitchen, her Sundays, the particular quality of light through her window while something browned on the stove, and how when I cook now and reach for the butter dish I am reaching for her too, for all of them, the whole line of women who fed people because that's what love looked like, translated into something you could taste, something that made you close your eyes for just a second and go mmm, and how that mmm is the whole point, is joy distilled, is heritage you can hold in your hand, softened at room temperature, ready to become whatever it needs to become.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
